files.text:
The floor under the sand

The last few centimetres never come off with a spade. They come off with a trowel held almost flat, and then with brushes: a soft paintbrush, a hand brush with its bristles cut short, a pastry brush, anything that will not scratch. The sand is not swept away so much as pushed, a stroke at a time, into a low ridge at the side that someone lifts out with a dustpan and a bucket. The tesserae come up one by one, little cubes of limestone and marble and glass a centimetre across, set in lime mortar on a bed of crushed tile. Where the mortar has rotted they lie loose, and a careless stroke can lift them out of their places for good.

Dry, a floor is a disappointment. A film of dust lies in every joint, the stone is chalky, the reds come up pink and the blacks grey. So before the photographer climbs the ladder, someone goes over it with a sponge and a bucket, or a garden sprayer, and for a few minutes the floor looks as it did when it was new and polished: the colours come up dark and deep, the glass glints, and the picture can be read. Then it dries from the edges in. If the floor is to be lifted, its face is glued to cloth, the bedding is cut away beneath it in sections, and each piece is turned over, cleaned from the back and laid on a new support before it is turned face up again and the cloth is soaked off.

# excavation A Roman floor at the bottom of a trench, under a skin of sand and dust, and you uncover it with a brush. The sand does not vanish where you brush: it is pushed, building low ridges along both sides of every stroke and a little pile where a stroke ends, and a ridge heaped too steep slumps back down. Brushed clean, the stones come up dull and chalky under a veil of dust that keeps the marks of the bristles. Then you wet it, as excavators do before they photograph a floor: a press of the sponge lying by the trench (or two taps, or Enter) splashes water over the patch you have been working, and there the tesserae go dark, deep and glossy and the picture blazes into colour. Wet sand goes dark and sticks. Over about twenty seconds the patch dries from its edges in, back to dust. ```html ``` Give the figure a size (an `aspect-ratio` is easiest); the `` fills it with `object-fit: cover`, and any `object-position` you give it is the crop the floor uses. The sponge is optional: any `.ex-sponge` button inside the figure wets the floor when pressed. Or call `excavation(figure, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-depth` | `depth` | `7` | css px of sand over the floor, on average (thicker in drifts and against the walls) | | `data-brush` | `brush` | `1` | scales the brush: its width, so how much one stroke clears | | `data-hint` | `hint` | `.14 .8` | where the corner already brushed clean lies, as fractions of the figure; `none` for none | | `data-dry` | `dry` | `24` | seconds the heart of a splash takes to dry (its edges go first; it reads as wet for about 20 s) | | `data-sand` | `sand` | `assets/sand.webp` | the grain: a seamless greyscale tile, power-of-two, mean grey | ## Using it - **Mouse or pen:** drag to brush. Back-and-forth scrubbing, as a person really brushes, works best. Double-click to wet the floor there. - **Touch:** a sideways stroke brushes at once; a finger held still for a quarter of a second brushes in any direction for that touch. Anything else scrolls the page (`touch-action: pan-y`), so the trench never traps a vertical swipe. Two quick taps wet the floor there. - **The sponge:** pressing it wets the middle of what you have brushed clean (or the middle of the floor if you have not started). - **Keyboard:** the figure is focusable. Enter or Space wets the middle of the floor; the arrow keys brush a short scrubbing stroke, moving across the floor. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--ex-sand` | `#c9b494` | loose sand, dry (the grain photo modulates it) | | `--ex-soil` | `#85705c` | the soil around the cut | | `--ex-dust` | `#dcd1bd` | the film of dust left on the stones | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | Wet sand and wet stone are derived from these, not themed separately. The canvas is transparent outside the ragged edge of the soil, so the page shows through. ## How it works - **Sand.** A height field on the CPU, about 300 cells on the long side (never finer than 2.5 css px), in css px, so slopes are real slopes. It starts as an even layer with some depth variation, wind ripples (a long gentle stoss and a short lee) that wander and fade, and sand slumped against the foot of the walls; the hint corner is made by running the real brush along a few wiggly strokes before the first frame. - **The brush** is a round, soft-edged footprint (1.7 R along the stroke, 2 R across, R 20-40 css px, weight `(1 - r²)^1.4`) that wobbles a little either side of the path, as a hand does, dragged along the pointer's path in steps shorter than a cell. Each step lifts a share of the sand under it, more under the middle of the bristles than at their tips, and throws it: a little just ahead of the brush, where the next step picks it up again, so a small mound travels in front and is left as a pile where the stroke ends, and the rest out to the side just past the bristles, a little further for a quick flick, which builds the ridges along the track. Excavators clear outward, so the throw is also bent toward the unexcavated side: each step reads the sand on a ring 1.8 R out, and the more one-sided it is (the brush is at the edge of a cleared patch), the more the sand goes toward the deep side. Thrown sand is fanned over an arc, not dropped in one spot, and sand thrown across bare floor keeps sliding until it meets standing sand: strokes inside a clearing all feed the one bank around it rather than leaving a ridge between every two strokes. Just outside the bristles, the splayed tips flick any spur left between two strokes outward onto that bank, so even rows of parallel back-and-forth strokes end in a soft, irregular oval with one continuous bank. Repeated strokes widen a clean field and bank the sand round its edge instead of back into it. Sand that would land on the trench wall stays put. Half of what is lifted is lost (the fine fraction, gone into the air and the dustpan). An elephant-sized area comes clean in six to ten back-and-forth strokes. - **Relaxation.** Every pair of neighbours (across, down and both diagonals) steeper than the angle of repose, 32 degrees, passes part of the excess downhill, symmetrically, four passes a frame over only the region still moving; slopes a little short of it creep, which rounds the crests of banks. A ridge heaped too steep visibly slumps over a fraction of a second. Wet sand holds a slope three times steeper and resists the brush. - **Dust.** A separate film under the sand. Bristles touch it only where the sand is already thin, thin it a little per pass and never quite clear it (it bottoms out at 16%), and leave it combed: the direction of the last strokes is kept per cell (as cos 2a, sin 2a, so back and forth agree) and the shader draws bristle streaks along it. - **Water.** A splash reaches out over a third of a second: five overlapping lobes with rims that wander with the ground, three runnels that run off down the floor's slight fall toward the lower right, and forty drops flung past the edge. The wet line is soft (about a tenth of a lobe), and wet sand is darker in its own hue with a slightly darker line where it meets dry sand; a wet film of sand over the stones goes see-through. It lays down most water at its heart and evaporates at an even rate, with a fixed patchy variation, so the patch dries from the edges in, as a real one does, and the loop stops when it is dry. - **Shader.** One pass draws everything. The floor, pre-cropped at one texel per device pixel: dry, the colour drained by 55% and the darks lifted halfway to white (dust in every pore: a pale, chalky floor that still reads); wet, saturation x1.65 in each stone's own hue and a gamma of 1.16 (whites stay a pale cream), the joints darkened (found as pixels darker than their neighbours), and a glint on every stone: a cell noise at the scale of the tesserae picks out the one stone in seven tilted toward the light, and only those carry a small, sharp glint; the joints stay matt. Over the whole wet area a broad, soft, low-gloss sheen, stronger toward the light. Over it the dust veil, which only ever lightens (it turns translucent when wet, which is why excavators wet a floor before they photograph it), and the sand: cover `1 - e^(-h / k)` with k varied by the grain, so a thin layer is grainy and see-through and a thick one opaque; albedo and micro relief from a real photograph of fine sand, sampled at two scales and angles so it never visibly repeats; lit from the height field's normals by a low warm light (36 degrees, from the upper left). Shadows are marched toward that light through the sand and the walls (14 steps, 36 px), with a penumbra that widens with distance, so ridges and the trench walls cast them. - **The trench.** Two signed distance fields, built once per size at half css resolution: the cut (a rectangle set off-centre, pushed about by long, slow noise and a few bites) and the ragged outer edge of the soil, so the bank is wide on one side and almost gone on another, but always a little outside the cut. The soil has pebbles (lit domes, each its own colour), a damper, darker strip just behind the cut, and in places it has crumbled and spilled into the trench as darker, thicker sand at the foot of the wall; the sand all along the foot of the walls is damp and darker too. The cut face is a 4-7 px slope from the floor to the soil top, 18-40 px up depending on the size of the panel, lit like everything else. ## Tuning The constants at the top of `excavation.js` are the physics: `REPOSE` (tan of the angle of repose), `K_LIFT` (how much a pass lifts), `KEEP` (how much of it lands again), `K_DUST` and `DUST_MIN` (the dust film), `RESIDUE` (sand the bristles always leave), `ELEV` and `LIGHT`. The brush width is `brushR()`. The dry and wet looks are `chalk()` and `wetten()` in the shader. A floor photographed straight down, with a lot of white ground and a strong dark figure, shows the effect best: the chalky dry state reads as dust, and the wet patch has somewhere to go. ## Behaviour and cost - **The loop runs only while something moves:** while brushing, while sand is still slumping, while a splash spreads, and while anything is wet (drying is updated about 20 times a second). Then it stops. Nothing runs off screen or in a hidden tab; a patch that is still wet when you scroll away waits for you. - Each frame re-uploads only the rows of the field that changed. Brushing costs a millisecond or two on a laptop; the shader is about 45 texture reads a pixel (mostly the shadow march), and it is drawn only when something changed. - Canvas DPR capped at 2. The floor image needs about 2x the panel's css width in pixels (the demo's is 2880 px wide). - Without WebGL, or if the image is cross-origin (WebGL refuses it), the `` stays, dusted by a CSS filter and clipped to a ragged edge. Print shows it too. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The image and canvas are decorative (`alt=""`, `aria-hidden`). The figure is focusable with `role="application"` and a label explaining the controls (unless you set your own). A polite live region says when the floor is wet. - The sponge is a real `
